sources.citation: Green, Christopher R. 2018. A survey of word-level replacive tonal patterns in Western Mande. Mandenkan 59: 67-108. DOI 10.4000/mandenkan.1420
sources.note: §4.1.2.1 Mokole, p. 82: Kuranko used as the Mokole exemplar because Kastenholz 1987 is 'the most extensive, published tonal description among these languages'; H/L tone melodies in compounds after Kastenholz 1987:157-162. Neither 'stress' nor 'accent' occurs in the paper.

sources.citation: Idiatov, Dmitry. 2017. Mande languages. Oxford Bibliographies in Linguistics (prefinal version).
sources.note: Annotated bibliography only: Kastenholz 1987 = 'A description of Koranko. One of the few available sources for the languages of the Mokole subgroup.'
Only source cited is Kastenholz 1987; no values for the stress features 14A-17A are shown for Koranko.

sources.citation: Vydrin, V. F. 2017. Манде языки [Mande languages]. In V. F. Vydrin, Yu. V. Mazurova, A. A. Kibrik & E. B. Markus (eds.), Языки мира: Языки манде, 16-45. St Petersburg: Нестор-История. (whole volume PDF, 1151 pp.)
sources.note: Family-level only, p. 34: 'Ударение в большинстве М.я. отсутствует. Там, где оно может быть выделено (в частности, бамана), его функциональная нагрузка невелика.' ('Stress is absent in most Mande languages; where it can be identified (in particular Bamana) its functional load is small.') and 'Практически все языки манде тональны'. The Koranko paragraph (pp. 19-20) gives only demography and 'grammar, dictionary and a small text corpus published by Raimund Kastenholz'. The volume has no Koranko article (index: 'Коранко язык → моколе группа'). Davydov's chapter 'Манден диалекты Гвинеи' (pp. 165-…

sources.citation: Vydrina, Alexandra. 2017. A corpus-based description of Kakabe, a Western Mande language: prosody in grammar. PhD thesis, INALCO, Paris. HAL tel-03203594
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: For Koranko: p. 45 'Only Koranko has a grammar and a dictionary (Kastenholz 1987a, 1987b)'; reproduces Kastenholz 1987b: 67 (vowel-length minimal pairs), 88-89 (citation-form pitch levels [332]/[232], final L of the article), 103-104; argues the Koranko article is a floating L, not H as Kastenholz claimed. No stress statement for Koranko; a two-level-tone language throughout.

sources.citation: Konoshenko, Maria. 2014. Studying tonal complexity, with a special reference to Mande languages. Language Documentation & Conservation 8: 563-586.
sources.note: Table 1 (p. 566): Koranko named as the Mokole example among the 22 Mande languages with 2 level tone contrasts. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Vydrine, Valentin. 2009. Esquisse de la langue lélé (groupe mokolé). Mandenkan 45: 29-104.
sources.note: Lele sketch with Koranko comparanda from Kastenholz 1987 (lexicostatistics p. 31; article rules 'plus simples qu'en koranko (Kastenholz 1987a, 193-206)'; fn. 9 Kastenholz assigns H tone to the Koranko article). Nothing on stress or accent for Koranko or Lele.

sources.citation: Kastenholz, Raimund. 1983. Note sur les marques prédicatives en koranko. Mandenkan 6: 55-73.
sources.note: Sierra Leone Koranko of Morofindugu (Mongo chiefdom), fieldwork 1982. Only tonal remarks: the demonstrative pán is 'prononcé avec un ton toujours distinctement haut' (n. 9) and an utterance boundary 'se manifeste... sur le plan tonal, par un downstep' (n. 11). Nothing on stress or accent. scanned at 300 dpi (no text layer).

sources.citation: Thomas, Northcote W. 1916. Specimens of languages from Sierra Leone. London: Harrison & Sons.
sources.note: Koranko wordlist recorded through Temne (p. 34ff.); the 'Tones' section (pp. 61-62) covers Bulom and Loko only. Nothing on Koranko accent.
